Appendix A Metric and solver taxonomy tables

For reference, we collect here the two taxonomy tables from the framework sections of the main text: table 6 enumerates the three metric instantiations (section 4), and table 7 the (metric, solver) cells we evaluate (section 5).

Appendix B Activation extraction and dataset construction

We extract residual-stream activations from Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) at layer 28 and the last-prompt-token position, using the causalab baseline pipeline (Wurgaft et al., 2026) to standardize prompts and counterfactuals across tasks. For each of the four tasks (weekdays, months, letters, ages) the prompt template is the arithmetic form What is kk {units} after zz?, with kk drawn uniformly from the task-specific support and zz drawn from the conceptual domain 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. Per-task prompt counts (after a 55-paraphrase augmentation that increases corpus size without changing the (entity,number)(\text{entity},\text{number}) semantic content) are: weekdays 245245, months 420420, letters ∼450{\sim}450, ages ∼4,400{\sim}4{,}400 capped at 1,0001{,}000 for tractability. Train/test split is 80/2080/20 deterministic on seed 4242; carrier-prompt sampling at evaluation time is re-seeded per pair on seed 4242 so within-pair carrier sets are reproducible.

Appendix C PHATE diffusion-distance configuration

We supervise GAGA’s distance-matching loss with PHATE diffusion-potential distances (Moon et al., 2019) computed on the raw 4096-dimensional residual-stream activations. PHATE proceeds in three stages: (a) build a kk-nearest-neighbor graph over the activations using Euclidean distance; (b) compute the random-walk transition matrix and raise it to a diffusion time tt; (c) define the diffusion potential ϕi=−log⁡Pi,⋅t\phi_{i}=-\log P^{t}_{i,\cdot} and take pairwise Euclidean distances between potentials. We use the reference implementation (phate package), with k=15k=15, tt chosen by the von Neumann entropy heuristic, no landmark approximation (since per-task corpora are small enough to admit dense computation), and L2 normalization of activations prior to graph construction.22 2 L2 normalization is recommended by Moon et al. (2019) for high-dimensional embeddings whose magnitude is informationally redundant; LM residual streams qualitatively satisfy this. The output is a dense N×NN\times N distance matrix D=(di​j)D=(d_{ij}) that fixes the target geometry on which we will train the encoder.

Appendix D GAGA architecture and training

This appendix gives a self-contained description of how we adapt the Geometry-Aware Generative Autoencoder of Sun et al. (2025) to LM activations, with all design choices and hyperparameters specified.

Architecture.

The encoder ϕ\phi and decoder ψ\psi are MLPs:

ϕ:ℝ4096\displaystyle\phi:\;\mathbb{R}^{4096}\; →ℝ1024→ℝ512→ℝ256→ℝ128→ℝk\displaystyle\to\;\mathbb{R}^{1024}\;\to\;\mathbb{R}^{512}\;\to\;\mathbb{R}^{256}\;\to\;\mathbb{R}^{128}\;\to\;\mathbb{R}^{k}
ψ:ℝk\displaystyle\psi:\;\mathbb{R}^{k}\; →ℝ128→ℝ256→ℝ512→ℝ1024→ℝ4096\displaystyle\to\;\mathbb{R}^{128}\;\to\;\mathbb{R}^{256}\;\to\;\mathbb{R}^{512}\;\to\;\mathbb{R}^{1024}\;\to\;\mathbb{R}^{4096}

Each hidden layer is followed by BatchNorm and a ReLU; the latent and output projections are linear. The latent dimension kk is task-dependent: k=2k=2 for the four 1-D tasks (weekdays, months, letters, ages), and k=3k=3 for the ICLR grid/cylinder tasks of Park et al. (2025). We chose to embed in k=dintrinsic+1k=d_{\text{intrinsic}}+1 rather than k=dintrinsick=d_{\text{intrinsic}} so that periodic structures (cyclic concepts) can be embedded faithfully without antipodal collapse. The original GAGA targets gene-expression data in ℝ20∼50​k\mathbb{R}^{20{\sim}50\text{k}} with hidden widths [64,64,64][64,64,64]; our wider hidden layers reflect both the larger ambient dimension and the steeper Lipschitz behavior of LM residual streams.

Distance-matching loss.

The core supervision matches latent Euclidean distances to PHATE manifold distances:

ℒdist=𝔼i≠j​[(‖ϕ⁡(hi)−ϕ⁡(hj)‖2−di​j)2⋅e−α​di​j],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dist}}=\mathbb{E}_{i\neq j}\Bigl[\bigl(\|\phi(h_{i})-\phi(h_{j})\|_{2}-d_{ij}\bigr)^{2}\cdot e^{-\alpha\,d_{ij}}\Bigr], (7)

where α=0.1\alpha=0.1 controls a soft local-distance prior: the exponential weighting attenuates contributions from large di​jd_{ij}, focusing the encoder’s isometry constraint on local geometry, where the manifold tangent plane is a good approximation. With α=0\alpha=0 the loss recovers a global isometry target; with α→∞\alpha\to\infty only kk-NN distances are preserved.

Reconstruction and cycle losses.

The decoder is tied to the encoder with two further losses:

ℒrecon\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}} =𝔼i​[‖ψ⁡(ϕ⁡(hi))−hi‖22],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i}\bigl[\|\psi(\phi(h_{i}))-h_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr], (8)
ℒcycle\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cycle}} =𝔼i​[‖ϕ⁡(ψ⁡(ϕ⁡(hi)))−ϕ⁡(hi)‖22].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i}\bigl[\|\phi(\psi(\phi(h_{i})))-\phi(h_{i})\|_{2}^{2}\bigr]. (9)

ℒrecon\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}} is essential for our intervention pipeline: we steer by sampling waypoints in the latent space, decoding each through ψ\psi, and patching the result into the residual stream. A bad decoder yields “junk” patches even if the latent geometry is correct. ℒcycle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cycle}} is a stabilizer that ensures ϕ∘ψ≈id\phi\circ\psi\approx\mathrm{id} on the latent manifold, preventing the decoder from wandering off the encoder’s image (which would silently break the pullback-metric interpretation).

Total loss and weights.

The full objective is

ℒ=λd​ℒdist+λr​ℒrecon+λc​ℒcycle\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{d}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dist}}+\lambda_{r}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}}+\lambda_{c}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cycle}} (10)

with (λd,λr,λc)=(0.9,0.1,0.05)(\lambda_{d},\lambda_{r},\lambda_{c})=(0.9,0.1,0.05). These weights follow the original GAGA Stage-A recipe (Sun et al., 2025); we add the cycle term (absent in some early GAGA variants) because we observed that the decoder otherwise produces small-norm reconstructions that the LM treats as near-zero patches, suppressing rather than steering behavior.

Training procedure.

We sample mini-batches of B=256B=256 activations and form the dense B×BB\times B pairwise distance sub-matrix from the precomputed DD on each step (the point-cloud dataloader of Sun et al. (2025)). The model is trained with AdamW at learning rate 10−310^{-3}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}, and a linear-warmup-then-cosine schedule over up to 300300 epochs. Early stopping is triggered on a held-out 20% validation split using ℒdist\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dist}} alone, with a patience of 30 epochs. Final distance-matching accuracy is reported as 1−𝔼i≠j​[(‖ϕ⁡(hi)−ϕ⁡(hj)‖2−di​j)2]/Var⁡(di​j)1-\mathbb{E}_{i\neq j}\bigl[(\|\phi(h_{i})-\phi(h_{j})\|_{2}-d_{ij})^{2}\bigr]/\mathrm{Var}(d_{ij}) on the validation split. The per-encoder pb_demap_r column of tables 8 and 9 reports this distance-matching quality for the PCA(6464) variants on weekdays and months.

GAGA-PHATE vs. GAGA-Hellinger: two encoders, two distance sources.

We train two distinct GAGA encoders whose architectures and training procedures are identical except for the distance source {di​j}\{d_{ij}\} supervising eq. 7:

  • •

    GAGA-PHATE. di​j=d_{ij}= PHATE diffusion-potential distance on the raw 64-D PCA activations (Moon et al., 2019). The encoder pullback Jϕ⊤​JϕJ_{\phi}^{\!\top}J_{\phi} thus reflects activation-space density.

  • •

    GAGA-Hellinger. di​j=d_{ij}= Hellinger distance on per-prompt output distributions, di​j=12​‖pi−pj‖2d_{ij}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\|\sqrt{p_{i}}-\sqrt{p_{j}}\|_{2}. The encoder pullback is then trained to track behavioral similarity, and so approximates the behavior-side pullback metric GF=JF⊤​JF+ϵ​IG_{F}=J_{F}^{\!\top}J_{F}+\epsilon I of Wurgaft et al. (2026, Def. 1 eq. 7) much more closely than GAGA-PHATE does.

GAGA-Hellinger still differs from the analytical GFG_{F}: it pulls back from a 2-D latent rather than from the full simplex Δ|𝒵|\Delta^{|\mathcal{Z}|}, and its rank is capped at 22 regardless of |𝒵||\mathcal{Z}|. We treat GAGA-PHATE and GAGA-Hellinger as two cells in the methods grid of table 6.

Differences from Sun et al. (2025).

Three substantive deviations from the original GAGA: (1) wider hidden layers to accommodate the larger ambient dimension; (2) the cycle-consistency term described above; (3) PHATE / Hellinger distances are computed once and cached, rather than recomputed per epoch as in some GAGA variants for streaming data settings. We do not use GAGA’s Stage-B (warped metric with discriminator) or Stage-C (Langevin sampling), since our target is interpolation and intervention rather than generation.

Appendix E Geodesic Bridge: amortized geodesic computation

Given two activation endpoints h0,h1∈𝒜h_{0},h_{1}\in\mathcal{A}, the geodesic under our learned pullback metric is the minimizer of

arg⁡min⁡∫01π⁡‖Jϕ​(π⁡(t))​π˙​(t)‖2​𝑑t,π⁡(0)=h0,π⁡(1)=h1.\arg\min_{\pi}\;\textstyle\int_{0}^{1}\|J_{\phi}(\pi(t))\,\dot{\pi}(t)\|_{2}\,dt,\qquad\pi(0)=h_{0},\;\pi(1)=h_{1}. (11)

Rather than optimize this per pair, we use the parametric curve module GeodesicBridge of Sun et al. (2025), which learns an amortized curve generator cθc_{\theta}:

cθ​(h0,h1,t)=(1−t)​h0+t​h1+σq​(t)​MLPθ​(ϕ⁡(h0),ϕ⁡(h1),t),c_{\theta}(h_{0},h_{1},t)=(1-t)\,h_{0}+t\,h_{1}+\sigma_{q}(t)\,\mathrm{MLP}_{\theta}\!\bigl(\phi(h_{0}),\,\phi(h_{1}),\,t\bigr), (12)

where σq​(t)=1−(2​t−1)q\sigma_{q}(t)=1-(2t-1)^{q} is an envelope that vanishes at the endpoints (we use q=4q=4). MLPθ\mathrm{MLP}_{\theta} is a 4-layer MLP of width 256 with ReLU activations. The objective during training is the integrated length eq. 11 on a population of randomly sampled endpoint pairs from the training activations, optionally augmented by a density-weighted term that penalizes excursions through low-density regions:

ℒbridge​(θ)=𝔼(h0,h1)​[∫01‖Jϕ​(cθ​(t))​c˙θ​(t)‖2​𝑑t+μ​∫01ρ​(cθ​(t))−1​𝑑t],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bridge}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(h_{0},h_{1})}\!\Bigl[\int_{0}^{1}\|J_{\phi}(c_{\theta}(t))\,\dot{c}_{\theta}(t)\|_{2}\,dt+\mu\int_{0}^{1}\rho(c_{\theta}(t))^{-1}\,dt\Bigr], (13)

with ρ\rho a kernel-density estimate on the training activations and μ=0.05\mu=0.05. The first term is the length under the pullback metric; the second is the density-weighted term that keeps geodesics on-manifold even when the encoder Jacobian is locally near-singular. We train for 50,00050{,}000 steps with Adam at learning rate 10−310^{-3}, batches of 64 endpoint pairs, and a discretization of T=32T=32 time steps per curve.

Appendix F Autodiff geodesics: solver and analytical JFJ_{F} implementation

This appendix gives concrete implementation details for the two solver/metric ingredients introduced in sections 5 and 4.3: the L-BFGS free-waypoint solver, and the analytical JFJ_{F} metric used in its highest-fidelity instantiation.

F.1 Free-waypoint path parameterization

Given two fixed endpoints h0,h1∈𝒜h_{0},h_{1}\in\mathcal{A} and a number of discretization steps KK, the path is represented as

π=(π0,π1,…,πK),π0=h0,πK=h1,\pi=(\pi_{0},\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{K}),\qquad\pi_{0}=h_{0},\ \pi_{K}=h_{1},

with the K−1K-1 interior waypoints {π1,…,πK−1}\{\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{K-1}\} as the only optimized parameters. Initialization is the linear interpolation πk(0)=(1−k/K)​h0+(k/K)​h1\pi_{k}^{(0)}=(1-k/K)\,h_{0}+(k/K)\,h_{1}, so the optimization starts at the straight-line baseline. We use K=50K=50 throughout to match the steering resolution of Wurgaft et al. (2026). This is the parameterization the L-BFGS solver uses in practice; a Bernstein-basis Bézier variant with C=8C=8 control points yields qualitatively identical geodesics in preflight checks but has a marginally rougher length landscape and is not reported.

F.2 Discrete length functional and L-BFGS

Given a metric g⁡(h)=J​(h)⊤​J​(h)g(h)=J(h)^{\!\top}J(h) at each waypoint, the discrete length to minimize is

L⁡(π)=∑k=0K−1‖J⁡(πk)​Δk‖22+ϵ​‖Δk‖22,Δk=πk+1−πk,L(\pi)\;=\;\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\sqrt{\bigl\|J(\pi_{k})\,\Delta_{k}\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\;+\;\epsilon\,\|\Delta_{k}\|_{2}^{2}},\qquad\Delta_{k}=\pi_{k+1}-\pi_{k}, (14)

with ϵ\epsilon a small regularizer absorbing rank deficiency. The right-hand factored form keeps memory at O⁡(K⋅m⋅D)O(K\cdot m\cdot D) with m=rank⁡(J)≤|𝒵|+1≪Dm=\mathrm{rank}(J)\leq|\mathcal{Z}|+1\ll D, instead of the O⁡(K⋅D2)O(K\cdot D^{2}) that an explicit G=J⊤​JG=J^{\!\top}J matrix would require.

We use the freeze-metric approximation: at each L-BFGS iteration, J⁡(πk)J(\pi_{k}) is recomputed at the current waypoint but detached from the optimizer’s computation graph (Arvanitidis et al., 2018). Gradients therefore flow only through the Δk\Delta_{k} in the outer norm, not through the metric’s dependence on πk\pi_{k}. This is the standard discrete-Riemannian choice; it gives a Newton-like step on a frozen quadratic form and avoids the second-order gradient terms that would otherwise be required.

Optimizer settings: torch.optim.LBFGS with lr=1.0, max_iter=200, tolerance_grad=1e-6, tolerance_change=1e-6, history_size=20, and line_search_fn=‘strong_wolfe’. A single optimizer.step(closure) call runs the full 200200 internal iterations; interior waypoints are the only parameters, with endpoints re-attached via torch.cat at each closure evaluation. Gradient clipping at ‖g‖∞≤1.0\|g\|_{\infty}\leq 1.0 prevents the path-collapse failure mode mentioned in section 5.

F.3 Analytical JFJ_{F} metric

The metric specified in Wurgaft et al. (2026, Def. 1 eq. 7) is

GF​(h)=JF​(h)⊤​gy​JF​(h)+ϵ​I,G_{F}(h)\;=\;J_{F}(h)^{\!\top}\,g_{y}\,J_{F}(h)\;+\;\epsilon I,

where F:𝒜→𝒴F:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{Y} is the rest-of-the-network forward map (layer-28 activations to output distribution restricted to the concept domain plus an “other” bin). We compute this metric exactly, with the following choices.

Hellinger output coordinates make gy=Ig_{y}=I.

We define F⁡(h)=softmax⁡(logits⁡[𝒵∪{other}])F(h)=\sqrt{\mathrm{softmax}(\mathrm{logits}[\mathcal{Z}\cup\{\text{other}\}])}: the LM forward pass restricted to concept tokens, with ⋅\sqrt{\cdot} applied so that outputs live in Hellinger coordinates. Under this parameterization the natural behavior-space metric is the identity: gy=Ig_{y}=I, since Hellinger distance is Euclidean distance on p\sqrt{p}. GFG_{F} then reduces to JF⊤​JF+ϵ​IJ_{F}^{\!\top}J_{F}+\epsilon I.

Row-by-row Jacobian extraction.

JF∈ℝ(|𝒵|+1)×DJ_{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{(|\mathcal{Z}|+1)\times D} is computed row-by-row via torch.autograd.grad with retain_graph=True: one backward pass per concept-token output (plus one for the “other” bin), each producing one row of JFJ_{F}. We use this in preference to torch.func.jacrev or torch.func.jacfwd because their functionalization requirements interact awkwardly with the subspace-replacement injection (section F.4) of pre-computed PCA activations into a wrapped forward pass.

Carrier handling.

GFG_{F} is carrier-dependent: the rest-of-network tail attends to the carrier prompt’s context, so JF​(h)J_{F}(h) is defined relative to a prompt. For the L-BFGS optimization we pin a single canonical carrier — the first test-split prompt, shared across all centroid pairs; an expectation of JFJ_{F} over carriers is the costlier principled variant and is left to future work. Evaluation of EBCE_{\mathrm{BC}} at the resulting waypoints still averages over all 1616 carriers as for the other methods, so per-pair EBCE_{\mathrm{BC}} values remain directly comparable across methods.

ϵ\epsilon regularizer.

We default to ϵ=10−3\epsilon=10^{-3}. The rank cap rank⁡(JF)≤|𝒵|+1\mathrm{rank}(J_{F})\leq|\mathcal{Z}|+1 ensures that the unregularized JF⊤​JFJ_{F}^{\!\top}J_{F} is singular on the D−|𝒵|−1D-|\mathcal{Z}|-1 dimensional nullspace; ϵ​I\epsilon I on this nullspace defines a small but nonzero length on directions invisible to FF, which prevents the path from escaping into that nullspace under optimization. Sensitivity to ϵ\epsilon is reported on a long-hop pair in appendix H.

Compute.

∼\sim33 GPU-minutes per pair on a single A100 for weekdays (|𝒵|=7|\mathcal{Z}|=7); larger concept schemas cost proportionally more. For comparison, GAGA encoder Jacobian extraction is ∼30\sim 30 seconds per pair, and the GeodesicBridge inference is ∼50\sim 50 milliseconds per pair — the learned surrogate is by far the cheaper metric to evaluate. We report the analytical-GFG_{F} cell on weekdays (all 2121 centroid pairs).

F.4 Subspace-replacement injection

All optimization happens in the PCA(64) subspace, but the LM expects ℝ4096\mathbb{R}^{4096} activations. For a waypoint πk∈ℝ64\pi_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{64} and a carrier prompt’s unintervened layer-28 last-token activation horig∈ℝ4096h_{\mathrm{orig}}\in\mathbb{R}^{4096}, the injected activation is

hinj=horig+(πk−P​horig)​P−1,h_{\mathrm{inj}}\;=\;h_{\mathrm{orig}}\;+\;(\pi_{k}-P\,h_{\mathrm{orig}})\,P^{-1},

implementing replacement of the in-PCA-subspace component while preserving the off-subspace component. In code, h_orig + (pi_k - h_orig @ pca.components_.T) @ pca.components_. This matches causalab’s FeatureInterpolateIntervention semantics and is the same lift used by all methods (linear, spline, GAGA, autodiff), so per-pair EBCE_{\mathrm{BC}} differences are purely method-attributable.

F.5 Comparison protocol

For each task and method, we compute paths over the same set of centroid pairs (all (N2)\binom{N}{2} for weekdays and months; 50 sampled pairs for letters and ages, seed 42) and report:

  • •

    Mean residual between paths after projecting both into the first three principal components of the activation distribution.

  • •

    Per-pair EBCE_{\mathrm{BC}} averaged across 16 carrier prompts, with paired tt-tests across methods on the per-pair EBCE_{\mathrm{BC}} arrays.

  • •

    Within-metric solver consistency: GAGA-PHATE + L-BFGS vs. GAGA-PHATE + Bridge under the same metric, expected to agree within 2×2\times on EBCE_{\mathrm{BC}} if both solvers converge.

The full metric-by-solver comparison table appears in table 7.

F.6 Spline as a degenerate special case

The spline geodesic of Wurgaft et al. (2026) can be recovered from eq. 14 by (a) restricting π\pi to the parametric spline family with control points at the labeled centroids; (b) replacing gg with the metric implicitly induced by the spline’s path-length functional; (c) replacing the optimization with closed-form interpolation through the (label-ordered) centroids. Removing each of these restrictions in turn defines an intermediate baseline. We report only the fully unrestricted autodiff variant in the main body; an ablation grid over the three restrictions is in appendix H.

Appendix G Encoder-variant ablation: PCA(64) GAGA encoders are inert

This appendix reports the full per-encoder matrix referenced from section 8.5 (15 PCA(6464) encoder variants ×\times 4 tasks, 11 rep, 55 shards/cell), tabulated in tables 8 and 9. Coverage at the time of writing: weekdays 15/1515/15, months 7/157/15 (GAGA-PHATE + Vanilla; GAGA-Hellinger and λ=10\lambda{=}10 not yet run); letters 0/150/15, ages 0/150/15 deferred (the GAGA-Out rows for letters/ages already lose EBCE_{\mathrm{BC}} to the baselines, so the PCA(6464) sweep there is lower priority). GAGA-Out rows are the frozen headline numbers (tables 2 and 3) reused as a reference, not re-run for this ablation. All numbers are mean across n=21n=21 pairs (weekdays) or n=50n=50 (months); paired-tt compares each encoder’s GAGA path against the linear baseline (more negative tt == more natural).

Reading the matrix.

Across two supervision targets (GAGA-PHATE, GAGA-Hellinger), seven λdist\lambda_{\mathrm{dist}} values from 0.10.1 to 500500, and the plain-reconstruction Vanilla-AE, every finished PCA(6464) encoder produces EBCE_{\mathrm{BC}} within ∼10−4\sim\!10^{-4} of the linear baseline, identical legibility (≈0.05\approx 0.05 weekdays, ≈0.13\approx 0.13 months), and identical endpoint target probability (0.0490.049 weekdays, 0.1280.128 months). The pb​_​demap​_​r\mathrm{pb\_demap\_r} column shows that several encoders do learn the supervision distance reasonably well (e.g. GAGA-PHATE λ=0.1\lambda{=}0.1 on weekdays at r=0.69r\!=\!0.69), but learning the distance does not translate into steering, because the lifted PCA(6464) endpoint is not an activation the language model would naturally produce for the target class. Only the raw-40964096 GAGA-Out encoder (where the geodesic, the lift, and the model all live in the same ambient space) separates from the baselines on every metric. The months GAGA-Hellinger family and the letters/ages PCA(6464) sweeps are left to future work; the GAGA-Out rows for letters/ages already lose EBCE_{\mathrm{BC}} to the baselines (table 2), so completing the PCA(6464) sweep there is unlikely to overturn the headline.

Appendix H Hyperparameter sensitivity

We report sensitivity of the headline number EBCE_{\mathrm{BC}} to: (1) latent dimension k∈{2,3,4}k\in\{2,3,4\}; (2) PHATE kkNN ∈{5,10,15,30}\in\{5,10,15,30\}; (3) GAGA decay rate α∈{0,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.5}\alpha\in\{0,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.5\}; (4) bridge density weight μ∈{0,0.01,0.05,0.1}\mu\in\{0,0.01,0.05,0.1\}. A full sensitivity sweep across these four hyperparameters is left to future work; pilot studies on weekdays indicated that the headline ordering is robust within reasonable ranges of each.

Appendix I Computational complexity

Table 10 compares the asymptotic cost of computing one geodesic between an endpoint pair, across the (metric, solver) cells of table 7. Let DD be the ambient activation dimension (D=4096D=4096), KK the number of path waypoints (K=50K=50), mm the rank of the metric Jacobian (m≤|𝒵|+1≪Dm\leq|\mathcal{Z}|+1\ll D), and TT the number of L-BFGS iterations. Write ℰ\mathcal{E} for the cost of one encoder forward-or-backward pass, ℱ\mathcal{F} for one forward-or-backward pass through the rest-of-network behaviour map FF (only the ∼3{\sim}3-layer tail downstream of the injection layer; section 4.3), and ℬ\mathcal{B} for one pass through the amortized bridge curve generator. The behaviour-map pass is far more expensive than the encoder pass: ℱ≫ℰ\mathcal{F}\gg\mathcal{E}.

Appendix J Additional figures

This appendix collects per-task path visualizations referenced from section 8, plus the GAGA-Out training-loss curves (fig. 2). Each figure projects activation-space trajectories onto the top principal components of the per-task training-prompt activation distribution, so visual comparisons across methods are made in the same coordinate frame. Linear paths appear as straight chords, the labeled cubic spline as a smooth curve through every class centroid, and the GAGA geodesic as the decoded output of the trained GeodesicBridge module evaluated at K=50K=50 time steps. Where multiple paraphrases of the same prompt are shown, each paraphrase’s unintervened layer-28 activation contributes its own off-subspace component during the lift back to ℝ4096\mathbb{R}^{4096} (section F.4), so different paraphrases trace slightly different 4096-D trajectories even though they all share the same in-PCA-subspace waypoints.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
